new_statements.quote: As already noted in §2.2.2, tone is distinctive in Grassfields languages and, as such, has been marked in the data. For the sake of space, this has been done on the vocalic segments using the diacritics [...] to represent high, mid, low, and related contour (rising and falling) tones. Because a proper tone analysis has not been done on any of these languages other than Aghem, the marking system should not be looked on as anything more than an impression of pitch.
new_statements.citation: Thormoset, David. 2007. Phonological reconstruction and the Aghem central vowels. MA thesis, University of Calgary. xii+153 pp. (also posted by SIL Cameroon; our bibliography dates it 2000/2006)
new_statements.locator: p. 60 (§3.1, data presentation; p. 68 of the silcam copy we hold); supporting: p. 41 (§2.2.2), p. 35 (§2.2 scope)
new_statements.relation_note: Treats all five A810 languages, Bu included, as tone languages and tone-marks the Bu data (H, M, L, contours) while warning that no tone analysis exists for Bu; p.41: 'Grassfields languages, like the majority of Bantu, are tonal' and floating tones cannot be reconstructed for the non-Aghem languages for lack of frame data; also gives Bu phonotactics (p.62: Bu allows only three coda consonants; p.75: 'Bu does not permit /n/ in coda'; Bu infinitive prefix e-). 'Stress' occurs only in diachronic speculation about Pre-Bantu/Aghem stem-initial stress (pp. 23, 63, 134), not as a synchronic claim about Bu.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bu (Laimbue), like the other West Ring A810 languages, is treated as a tone language with lexically distinctive tone; the thesis marks surface pitch (H/M/L/contours) on its Bu wordlist but makes no phonemic tone analysis and no statement about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Author cautions that mid-tone marks are impressionistic ('not an assertion that these languages have a fundamental mid tone -- they likely do not') and that floating tones could not be established outside Aghem.
new_statements.identity_note: Not a new discovery -- already held and read (READALL 2026-09-18, tag 'read: silent on stress'); re-listed here because A's search was for stress OR tone and this is the only opened work with first-hand Bu data and a tone remark whose scope includes Bu. p.35 §2.2: 'The primary focus of this study is the data from Aghem, Bu, Isu, Weh and Zhoa' (SIL Africa Area 1700-item wordlists recorded Jan 2004 by Nelson Tschonghongei & D. Thormoset for the Aghem Language Development Committee); p.4/ALCAM 810 'Aghem, Bu (Laimbu), Cha', Isu..'. Bu here = the Laimbwe village south of Wum (A810/West Ring), not Lower Fungom Buu. Glottolog has the work (West Ring table, tagged under Aghem, listed by Glottolog as an overview/comparative), not under laim1240.

new_statements.quote: The West Ring subgroup of Grassfields Bantu includes five varieties, Aghem, Bu, Isu, Weh, and Zoa [...] Most WR languages have two contrastive level tones (H vs L) plus a phonemic downstep marked by [ꜜ] and three phonemic contour tones: rising LH /ˇ/ vs falling from H to L /ˆ/ vs falling from H to downstepped H /'/. [gap: words naming the varieties concerned] tone systems, which operate a three-way contrast of level tones, i.e. H vs M vs L. [...] [Conclusion:] WR languages are remarkable for the following features: large vowel inventories which outnumber the five or seven vowel systems in Narrow Bantu; tone systems which operate contrasts beyond the two-way opposition of high vs low; an incipient transition in the noun class system from prefix marking to enclitic marking [...]
new_statements.citation: Kießling, Roland. 2025. West Ring (Grassfields Bantu). In Lutz Marten, Ellen Hurst-Harosh, Nancy C. Kula & Jochen Zeller (eds.), The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages, 717-729. Oxford: Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0060
new_statements.locator: §60.1 Introduction, p. 717 (chapter's first page; the tone sentence ends at the page footer) and Conclusion section (c. p. 728); text seen only as Google Books preview snippets
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. Kiessling 2025 lists Bu (= Laimbwe/Laimbue, confirmed by the held Kah 2016 'Bu and Laimbwe' text and Glottolog West Ring classification) among five WR varieties, but the tone sentence is 'Most WR languages have two contrastive level tones..' and the snippet gap hides which varieties have H/M/L; subgroup-level, from preview snippets only. | checker: Record: Google Books feed volume wfCFEQAAQBAJ 'The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages' (Marten, Hurst-Harosh, Kula, Zeller; OUP 2025-08-19; viewability view_partial) plus the CrossRef record already in the mirror (doi 10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0060) — exists, closed access (login) and a chapter-length…
new_statements.relation_note: Tone: WR (incl. Bu) = tone languages; majority system H/L + downstep + 3 contour tones; some with H/M/L. No stress statement seen. Only preview snippets read; full text closed (login).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The West Ring varieties, Bu (Laimbue) explicitly among them, are tone languages: most have two contrastive level tones (H, L) plus phonemic downstep and three phonemic contour tones (rising LH, falling HL, falling H-ꜜH); some WR variety/varieties (named in words not recoverable from the snippets) have a three-way level contrast H/M/L; the Conclusion generalises that WR tone systems 'operate contrasts beyond the two-way opposition of high vs low'. Nothing about word stress/accent in the recovered text.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in the recovered text
new_statements.exceptions: Some varieties have H vs M vs L instead of H vs L (+downstep); which ones could not be recovered (the words between footnote mark 7 and 'tone systems' on p. 717). Whether Bu is in the two-level majority or the three-level group is therefore NOT settled by what was read.
new_statements.identity_note: ROUND1-REOPENED (partially, text route): round 1 had only the CrossRef abstract of this closed-access chapter (Glottolog's current Glottolog's most extensive description for laim1240). 450 words of the chapter VERBATIM from Google Books preview snippets (GData feed, volume wfCFEQAAQBAJ, view_partial; c. 40 phrase-chained queries): the §60.1 Introduction incl. the vowel/tone paragraph on p. 717 and the Conclusion's feature list. The chapter treats the five West Ring varieties 'Aghem, Bu, Isu, Weh, and Zoa'; Bu = Laimbue [lmx] (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description note; Kießling 2021 n.1: 'Laimbue' is a rendering of the Bu phrase láim bù è 'the language of Bu'); not the Lower Fungom Bu/Buu. Full chapter not opened (OUP subscription; Unpaywall: closed; books.google.com HTML captcha-could not be reached by automated download). | New (2025) open Festschrift chapter found through the DNB SRU catalogue; not in Glottolog's laim1240/West Ring lists, ITEM, ROUND1 or A. 'Bu' here = the West Ring language (Laimbue [lmx]) as in Kießling's other work, not Lower Fungom Buu; but the chapter's evidence is Isu (isum1240), hence another-variety.
